passages.title: Do not take My enemies as allies
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat were revealed because of a single letter — written not by a hypocrite but by a sincere Companion who fought at Badr, and who tried to buy safety for his family by doing a favour to the enemies of Allah. Around that one incident Allah lays down a principle and then dismantles the motive behind it: ayah 1 forbids taking those enemies as trusted allies and warns that secret affection is not secret from Allah; ayah 2 shows what those same people would do to the believers if they ever got the chance; ayah 3 removes the very reason the compromise was made — the relatives and children for whose sake a person bends will be no use to him on the Day of Judgment.

## The letter that occasioned the Surah

Ibn Kathir opens his commentary by saying plainly that the story of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah is the reason behind the revelation of the beginning of this honourable Surah.

Hatib was among the Early Emigrants and had fought at Badr. He had children and wealth still in Makkah, but he was not of Quraysh — he was an ally of 'Uthman. Ma'arif ul Qur'an fills in why that mattered so much: the Muslims left behind in Makkah were being persecuted, and Emigrants who had relatives there enjoyed some degree of protection for their families through those ties. Hatib, originally from Yemen and with no relatives of his own in Makkah, had no such shield over his family.

When the people of Makkah broke the treaty of Hudaybiyah, the Prophet ﷺ ordered the Muslims to mobilise their forces for Makkah, and he prayed:

> "O Allah! Keep our news concealed from them."

Hatib saw an opening. Ma'arif ul Qur'an, drawing on Qurtubi (with reference to Qushairi and Tha'labi), records that a Makkan singer named Sarah had come to Madinah destitute after Badr — she told the Prophet ﷺ that she had neither migrated nor accepted Islam, but that her livelihood in Makkah had collapsed after the leaders of Quraysh were killed at Badr, and she had come for help. The Prophet ﷺ encouraged Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib to assist her; they helped her with money, clothing and other things and sent her off. Hatib wrote his letter to the people of Makkah, telling them of the Prophet's ﷺ intention to march on them, and dispatched it with her. His calculation was that a favour now would leave the Makkans indebted to him, and they would take care of his family. Ma'arif ul Qur'an notes he was sure Allah would grant His Messenger ﷺ victory regardless — he thought leaking the secret would not harm the Prophet ﷺ or Islam.

Allah told His Messenger ﷺ. Ibn Kathir makes the connection explicit: Allah conveyed this matter to him **because He had accepted the Prophet's ﷺ invocation** that their news be concealed. The prayer was answered by exposing the one man who had broken the secrecy.

## The pursuit

Imam Ahmad recorded from 'Ali that Allah's Messenger ﷺ sent him with two others, saying:

> "Proceed until you reach Rawdat Khakh, where there is a lady carrying a letter. Take that letter from her."

'Ali said: "So we proceeded on our way, with our horses galloping, until we reached the Rawdah." They found her and said, "Take out the letter." She said, "I am not carrying a letter." They said, "Take out the letter, or else we will take off your clothes." Then she produced it. (In Ibn Kathir's wording she took it out of her braid; the version in Ma'arif ul Qur'an says from her loincloth. The two commentaries also differ slightly on the riders: Ibn Kathir's narration names 'Ali, Zubayr and Al-Miqdad; Ma'arif ul Qur'an, citing the narration in the two Sahihs on 'Ali's authority, names 'Ali, Abu Marthad and Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam.)

The letter was brought to the Prophet ﷺ, who said only:

> "O Hatib! What is this?"

Hatib's answer is worth reading slowly: "O Allah's Messenger! Do not make a hasty decision about me. I was a person not belonging to Quraysh, but I was an ally to them. All the Emigrants who were with you have kinsmen who can protect their families. So I wanted to do them a favour, so they might protect my relatives, as I have no blood relation with them. I did not do this out of disbelief or to renegade from my religion, nor did I do it to choose disbelief after Islam."

The Prophet ﷺ said to his Companions, "Regarding him, he has told you the truth."

'Umar said, "O Allah's Messenger! Allow me to chop off the head of this hypocrite!" And the Prophet ﷺ replied:

> "He attended Badr. What can I tell you, perhaps Allah looked at those who attended Badr and said, 'O people of Badr, do what you like, for I have forgiven you.'"

Ma'arif ul Qur'an adds the human ending: hearing this, tears rolled down from 'Umar's eyes and he said, "Allah and His Messenger ﷺ alone has the knowledge of reality."

Ibn Kathir reports the story as collected in the Two Sahihs, and the narration through 'Ali as collected by the Group with the exception of Ibn Majah, through various chains that included Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah. He also preserves the scholars' scrupulousness about how much of the revelation belonged to the report itself: Al-Bukhari adds, in the chapter on the Prophet's battles, "Then Allah revealed the Surah, *O you who believe! Take not My enemies and your enemies as protecting friends*"; elsewhere Al-Bukhari records 'Amr, one of the narrators, saying the ayah was revealed about Hatib "but I do not know if the Ayah was mentioned in the Hadith"; and Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, asked the same question, said only, "This is the narration that I collected from 'Amr, I did not leave a letter out of it. I do not know if anyone else memorized the same words for it." That refusal to claim more than one knows is itself part of what the reader is being taught.

## Two verdicts held at once

Notice what does *not* happen. The Prophet ﷺ accepts Hatib's excuse — Ibn Kathir says explicitly that this is why he accepted it: because Hatib only wanted to have a favour on the Quraysh, on account of the property and family members he had left behind in Makkah. When 'Umar called him a hypocrite, the Prophet ﷺ did not endorse the word; he told his Companions, "Regarding him, he has told you the truth." His sincerity and his Badr were honoured.

And still the Qur'an came down to correct him. Mercy toward the man and correction of the act sit together in one episode. Ma'arif ul Qur'an says clearly that the position Hatib took was inappropriate — he was wrong in his thinking that if he did them a favour they would be obliged to him and take care of his family, because they were enemies of the faith.

## "My enemy and your enemy" — why these words

Ma'arif ul Qur'an draws attention to the wording. Allah does not say "do not take the *kuffar* — the disbelievers — as allies" here; He says **'aduwwī wa 'aduwwakum**, "My enemy and your enemy." Ma'arif ul Qur'an reads that choice of expression as an indication of the underlying cause of the injunction: hopes of friendship from your enemy and Allah's enemy are illusory. It is also an indication, it says, that an infidel, as long as he is an infidel, can never be a friend of a Muslim as long as he is a Muslim — and it puts it as a question you cannot answer: an infidel is the enemy of Allah, whereas a Muslim loves Allah; how can there be an intimate friendship between the two? Unless — Allah forbid — one loses one's faith, that intimacy is illusory and virtually impossible.

The word forbidden is **awliyā'** (singular *walī*), which Ibn Kathir renders as protecting friends: Allah has forbidden the believers to take them "as friends, supporters or companions." And Ibn Kathir defines the people concerned precisely: the idolaters and disbelievers **who are combatants** against Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the believers — those whom Allah has decided should be our enemies and should be fought. He gathers the parallel commands to show how consistent the Qur'an is here: 5:51, 5:57, 4:144, and 3:28 — the last of which itself contains the exception, "except if you indeed fear a danger from them."

Then the ayah describes what that alliance looked like in practice: **tulqūna ilayhim bil-mawaddah** — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "showing affection towards them," and by Ma'arif ul Qur'an as "expressing love with them." Ma'arif ul Qur'an says of the letter itself that writing such a letter to the disbelievers amounted to having friendly intimacy with them.

## The clauses of ayah 1, one by one

**"…while they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth."** Ma'arif ul Qur'an notes that *al-haqq* (the truth) here refers either to the Qur'an or to Islam, and that this clause names their rejection of the truth as the real reason for their enmity.

**"…and have driven out the Messenger and yourselves."** Ibn Kathir says this follows the encouragement to fight them and avoid being their supporters — because they expelled the Messenger ﷺ and his Companions on account of their hatred for Tawhid, which Ibn Kathir here pairs with the phrase that explains it: worshipping Allah alone in sincerity.

**"…because you believe in Allah, your Lord."** Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is piercing: *your only fault is that you believed in Allah, Lord of all that exists.* He points to the same note struck in 85:8, "they had no fault except that they believed in Allah," and 22:40, "those who have been expelled from their homes unjustly only because they said: Our Lord is Allah." Ma'arif ul Qur'an makes the same point: they were driven out not for any worldly grudge, but for one and only one reason — their faith.

**"If you have come forth to strive in My cause and to seek My good pleasure."** Ibn Kathir reads this as a condition put to the conscience: *if you are as described here* — if your migration really was for My cause and My pleasure — then do not take My enemies and yours as protecting friends, after they expelled you from your homes and property in rage against you and rejection of your religion. Ma'arif ul Qur'an draws out the implication: if the migration was indeed for the sake of Allah and His good pleasure, it is impossible for an infidel, the enemy of Allah, to take care of Allah's friend.

**"You show friendship to them in secret, while I am All-Aware of what you conceal and what you reveal."** Ibn Kathir turns this into a question addressed to the heart: do you do this, while I know the secrets of the hearts, the intentions and all apparent things? Ma'arif ul Qur'an adds that anyone who secretly keeps up such intimacy should not imagine it will remain secret: Allah is fully aware of what people do secretly and openly — and the story itself proves it, since Allah informed His Messenger ﷺ by revelation and had the secret plot thwarted.

**"And whosoever of you does that, then indeed he has gone astray from the straight path."** The Qur'an's own verdict on the act is not that it was a small slip. It is straying from the straight path.

## Ayah 2 — the test of "if they had the chance"

Ayah 2 answers Hatib's calculation on its own terms. He was banking on gratitude. Allah tells him what these people are actually like: **"Should they gain the upper hand over you, they would behave to you as enemies, and stretch forth their hands and their tongues against you with evil."**

Ibn Kathir: if they gain the upper hand over you, they would use every type of harm in their disposal to hurt you in words and action. Ma'arif ul Qur'an says the verse indicates how bitter the feelings of the disbelievers are towards the Muslims: they would use all means, their hands and their tongues, and would spare no effort to harm the Muslims — so it is impossible that, if they ever found their opportunity and overpowered the Muslims, they would exercise tolerance towards them. Hands and tongues together: violence and slander, the physical and the reputational.

**"And they desire that you should disbelieve."** Ibn Kathir explains: they are eager that you do not earn any good at all — their enmity to you is outward and inward. Then he asks the question the passage is built to provoke: *so how can you become supporters of this type of people?* Ma'arif ul Qur'an adds the sting: the greatest desire of the non-believers' hearts is to see the Muslims revert to disbelief, so when the Muslims stretch out a hand of friendship it will be at the cost of their belief; they will never be happy with the Muslims unless they give up their faith.

## Ayah 3 — the ties for which people compromise

Now the motive itself is taken away. **"Neither your relatives nor your children will benefit you on the Day of Resurrection. He will judge between you."**

Ma'arif ul Qur'an says this ayah refutes Hatib's plea directly: he did what he did for the love of his children — and they will be of no help on the Day of Resurrection. All relations on that day will come to an end; parents will flee from their children and children from their parents, and no secret will ever remain hidden from Allah.

Ibn Kathir gives the principle underneath it: your family relations will not benefit you with Allah if Allah decided to cause harm your way; they will not benefit you if you please them with what angers Allah. Those who agree with their family being disbelievers in order to please them "will have earned loss and failure and their deeds will be rendered invalid" — and their relation will not benefit them with Allah even if that relation were with a Prophet. He then cites the narration of Anas, recorded by Imam Ahmad and also collected by Muslim and Abu Dawud, in which a man asked the Prophet ﷺ where his father was and was told, "In the Fire" — and as the man turned away the Prophet ﷺ called him back and said, "Verily, my father and your father are in the Fire." Nothing gentler could have made the point: lineage does not transfer salvation, not even the noblest lineage on earth.

The passage closes with **"And Allah is the All-Seer of what you do."** A passage that began with a hidden letter ends with that reminder — and, as Ma'arif ul Qur'an says on this very ayah, no secret will ever remain hidden from Allah.

## What the passage asks of us

**Locate your loyalty before you locate your interests.** Hatib's error was not disbelief — he said so himself, and the Prophet ﷺ confirmed he was telling the truth. It was letting fear for his family set his loyalties for one moment. That is a live temptation for anyone with something to lose.

**Do not assume secrecy.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an states it plainly: no one who keeps a friendly intimacy with the enemies of the faith quietly should think it will stay quiet. Allah is fully aware of what people do secretly and openly.

**Judge the boundary correctly.** Ibn Kathir defines the people in question as the idolaters and disbelievers who are combatants against Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the believers, and among the ayat he gathers is 3:28 with its allowance, "except if you indeed fear a danger from them." Notice also where the sources place this episode: in the very lead-up to it, the Prophet ﷺ encouraged Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib to help a destitute Makkan woman who had neither migrated nor accepted Islam — with money, clothing and other things — before she was sent on her way.

**Be as fair to people as the Prophet ﷺ was to Hatib.** He heard the man out, declined to take up 'Umar's word "hypocrite," and weighed a lifetime — Badr — against one grave mistake. The passage corrects an act without discarding a man.

**Invest in the only tie that carries weight.** Relatives and children are dear, and Hatib's love for his children is exactly what the ayah addresses; but on the Day when He judges between you, they cannot help you. The relationship worth protecting at any cost is the one with Allah.

passages.title: Abraham's disavowal as the pattern to follow
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Ibn Kathir opens by telling us who is being addressed: Allah the Exalted is speaking to His faithful servants, "whom He commanded to disown the disbelievers, to be enemies with them, and to distance themselves and separate from them." Ayat 4–6 then hold up Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and the believers with him as the working model: what they said, where the line was drawn, and — just as importantly — the prayer that followed.

What binds the three ayat together is a single frame, repeated. Ayah 4 opens *qad kānat lakum uswatun ḥasanah* — "you already have an excellent example" — and ayah 6 says it again, *laqad kāna lakum fīhim uswatun ḥasanah*. Ibn Kathir reads that second statement as Allah asserting again what He had already said, now with the exception folded in. Everything between the two statements is the content of the example: a declaration (ayah 4), one thing carved out of it (the end of ayah 4), and a du'a (end of ayah 4 into ayah 5).

## Who is being addressed, and about what

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same conclusion Ibn Kathir does: this ayah "supports and emphasizes the abstaining from maintaining close friendly relations with non-believers," and the rule is illustrated by the example of Ibrahim, whose entire family worshipped idols — yet he not only washed his hands of them and disowned them, but announced, and erected a wall of, enmity and hatred with them.

That last detail is worth sitting with before anything else. The model Allah chooses is not a man who broke with strangers. It is a man who broke with his own household.

Note also who the example includes. Allah says "Ibrahim **and those with him**" — Ibn Kathir explains this as "his followers who believed in him." The example is not the prophet standing alone; it is him together with the believers around him.

## "Verily, we are free from you" — the declaration, phrase by phrase

Ibrahim's statement in ayah 4 comes in stages, and Ibn Kathir takes them one at a time.

**"Innā buraʼā'u minkum" — "we are free from you."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is one phrase: *we disown you*. And, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses, this was announced — said out to the people, not merely held inwardly.

**"Wa mimmā taʿbudūna min dūni-llāh" — "and from whatever you worship besides Allah."** The disavowal names two things: the people, and what they worship. It was never merely social.

**"Kafarnā bikum" — "we have rejected you."** Ibn Kathir's gloss: *we disbelieve in your religion and way*.

**"Wa badā baynanā wa baynakumu-l-ʿadāwatu wa-l-baghḍā'u abadan" — "and there has appeared between us and you hostility and hatred forever."** This is the hardest line in the passage, and Ibn Kathir's explanation of it is precise: "Animosity and enmity have appeared between us and you from now **and as long as you remain on your disbelief**; we will always disown you and hate you."

That qualification is not a softening; it is the actual sense of the sentence, because the ayah does not stop there.

**"Ḥattā tu'minū billāhi waḥdah" — "until you believe in Allah alone."** Ibn Kathir: *unless, and until, you worship Allah alone without partners and disbelieve in the idols and rivals that you worship besides Him.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point about Ibrahim — the enmity and hatred stand "forever, **unless and until** they give up idol-worship and have belief in Allah alone."

So "forever" and "until" sit in the same breath. The enmity has no expiry date and no negotiated middle ground — and yet, on both commentators' reading, it is tied to a condition: it stands as long as they remain on disbelief. It is directed at a stance. The door named in the ayah — *ḥattā tu'minū* — is the door Ibrahim himself is holding open while he speaks.

## The one thing not to imitate

Then comes an exception, and it is startling: *illā qawla Ibrāhīma li-abīhi la-astaghfiranna lak* — "except the saying of Ibrahim to his father: 'I will surely ask forgiveness for you, but I have no power to do anything for you before Allah.'"

Allah presents Ibrahim as the model to copy, and then, in the same ayah, marks off one act of his and says: not this.

Ibn Kathir's summary: "you have a good example in Ibrahim and his people; as for Ibrahim's prayer for his father, it was a promise that he made to his father." And when Ibrahim became sure that his father was an enemy of Allah, he declared himself innocent of him.

**Why this exception was needed.** Ibn Kathir supplies the background. Some of the believers used to invoke Allah for their parents who had died as disbelievers, begging Him to forgive them — and they did so claiming that Ibrahim used to invoke Allah to forgive his father. Allah replied in Sūrat al-Tawbah, in words addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and to those who believe:

> "It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask Allah's forgiveness for the idolators, even though they be of kin, after it has become clear to them that they are the dwellers of the Fire. And Ibrahim's request for his father's forgiveness was only because of a promise he made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he dissociated himself from him." (9:113–114)

So the clause in ayah 4 is closing off a specific misuse of the example. Ibn Kathir puts the meaning bluntly: *you cannot follow Ibrahim's example as proof in the case mentioned here, as being allowed to ask Allah to forgive those who died on shirk.* He notes that this is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, Muqātil bin Ḥayyān, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, "and several others."

Notice too what Ibrahim said in the same breath: *"but I have no power to do anything for you before Allah."* He did not promise an outcome. He promised only to ask — and said plainly that the outcome was not his to give.

## "Allaying a doubt" — how the scholars read the exception

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān devotes a section to the difficulty a careful reader will feel here, under the heading *Allaying a Doubt*. If Allah commands us to follow Ibrahim's model, and it is established in Sūrat al-Tawbah and elsewhere that he prayed for his idol-worshipping father, does that not permit praying for the forgiveness of idol-worshipping parents and other relatives? The answer given is that the later part of ayah 4 is exactly the carve-out: it is imperative to follow Ibrahim's model **in all respects except this one**. His sunnah in this particular matter is not to be emulated.

As for *why* Ibrahim prayed at all, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two possibilities, explained in Sūrat al-Tawbah: either he prayed before the prohibitory injunction was ordained, or he prayed when he felt that faith had entered his father's heart. Either way, "when it became plain to him that he was Allah's enemy he washed his hands of him and disowned him" — *fa-lammā tabayyana lahu annahu ʿaduwwun lillāhi tabarra'a minh* (9:114).

**A grammatical reading, and what it opens up.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then reports that some of the scholars analyse *illā qawla Ibrāhīm* grammatically as an *istithnā' munqaṭiʿ* — which it defines as "exceptive sentence in which the exception is severed from, or wholly different in kind from, the general term." On that analysis, praying for his father's forgiveness is not contrary to the Abrahamic model at all: Ibrahim was under the impression that his father had become a Muslim, so he prayed for the forgiveness of a father he took to be a Muslim. Later, when he learnt the truth, he gave up praying for him and renounced him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a live consequence from this, citing Qurṭubī: if anyone believes, even today, that a particular unbeliever has most probably embraced Islam, there is no harm in praying for his pardon. The section then ends where such matters should end — *Allah knows best.*

Two readings, then, both preserved rather than one crushing the other: on the first, the prayer is a real exception excluded from the model; on the second, it never belonged to the model in the first place, because Ibrahim was praying for someone he took to be a believer. What both agree on is the ruling: forgiveness is not sought for one who has died upon shirk.

## The prayer that follows the break

Here the passage turns. Ibn Kathir frames it: Ibrahim and his companions, who parted with their people and disowned their way, said afterwards — "while invoking Allah in humility and submission" — this:

**"Rabbanā ʿalayka tawakkalnā wa ilayka anabnā wa ilayka-l-maṣīr"** — "Our Lord! In You we put our trust, to You we turn in repentance, and to You is the final return."

Ibn Kathir: *we trust in You for all matters, we surrender all of our affairs to You, and to You is the final return in the Hereafter.*

Read the sequence Ibn Kathir lays out. The parting comes first; and what follows it, immediately, is not defiance but humility and submission. *Tawakkul* — trusting Allah for all matters, surrendering every affair to Him. *Inābah* — turning back to Him in repentance. *Maṣīr* — the final return, in the Hereafter.

## "Do not make us a fitnah for the disbelievers" (ayah 5)

The word *fitnah* covers trial and affliction, and the early authorities Ibn Kathir cites read the request along two closely related lines.

**Mujāhid:** "Do not punish us by their hands, nor with a punishment from You" — or they will say, "Had these people been following the truth, the torment would not have struck them." Ibn Kathir notes that aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said something similar.

**Qatādah:** "Do not give the disbelievers victory over us, thus subjecting us to trials by their hands. Surely, if You do so, they would then think that they were given victory over us because they are on the truth." Ibn Kathir records that this is the meaning **Ibn Jarīr preferred**.

**Ibn ʿAbbās**, in the report of ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah: "Do not give them dominance over us, lest we suffer trials by their hands."

Look closely at what is being feared in these reports. It is not simply pain. It is that the suffering would be misread as a verdict — that their defeat would be taken as evidence that the other side was on the truth. The prayer is protective of the truth itself, not only of their own comfort.

**"Waghfir lanā rabbanā"** — "and forgive us, our Lord." Ibn Kathir gives forgiveness two faces here: *cover our mistakes from being exposed to other than You, and forgive us for what sin is between us and You.* Concealment now; pardon then.

**"Innaka anta-l-ʿAzīzu-l-Ḥakīm"** — "Verily You, only You, are the Almighty, the All-Wise." Ibn Kathir glosses each name. On **al-ʿAzīz**: "and those who seek refuge in Your majesty are never dealt with unjustly." On **al-Ḥakīm**: wise "in Your statements, actions, legislation and decrees." So they ask for protection, and in the same sentence affirm that His decrees are wise ones.

## Ayah 6: said twice, and aimed carefully

*"Laqad kāna lakum fīhim uswatun ḥasanah"* — "Certainly there has been in them an excellent example for you to follow." Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah asserting again what He had stated before, with the exemption that was mentioned — the good example, minus the one clause carved out of it.

But the second statement adds something the first did not: *li-man kāna yarjū-llāha wa-l-yawma-l-ākhir* — "for whoever looks forward to Allah and the Last Day." Ibn Kathir says this is Allah "thus encouraging the believers who believe in Allah and the Return to Him."

So the example is set before everyone, and the ayah itself names who takes heart from it: those whose hope is fixed on meeting Allah and on the Last Day.

## "And whoever turns away"

*Wa man yatawalla* — and whoever turns away, Ibn Kathir says, meaning *from what Allah has ordained* — *fa-inna-llāha huwa-l-Ghaniyyu-l-Ḥamīd*, "then indeed Allah is al-Ghanī, al-Ḥamīd."

Ibn Kathir pairs this with another ayah: *"If you disbelieve, you and all on the earth together, then verily Allah is Ghanī, Ḥamīd"* (14:8).

On **al-Ghanī**, he reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, via ʿAlī bin Ṭalḥah: "the One Who is perfectly rich." That is Allah. Ibn Kathir adds: this is Allah's attribute that He alone is worthy of being described by; "surely, He has no equal, none like unto Him. All praise is due to Allah, the One, the Irresistible."

On **al-Ḥamīd**: the praiseworthy — praiseworthy "in all His statements and actions" — and, Ibn Kathir adds, there is no true god except Him alone.

This is where the passage lands. After a long call to a costly stand, the closing two names set the matter in proportion, and the ayah Ibn Kathir places beside them says it outright: were all the people of the earth to disbelieve together, Allah would still be Ghanī, Ḥamīd. Nothing is added to Him by our obedience, and nothing taken from Him by our turning away.

## Living it

The passage asks for a set of things it also models:

- **A break that is spoken, not merely felt.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Ibrahim announced it, and reads the ayah as establishing that a believer abstains from maintaining close friendly relations with those who reject faith — and that this held even for Ibrahim's own family.
- **A line drawn at religion, and a door left open.** The enmity in ayah 4 is tied by the ayah itself to a condition — *until you believe in Allah alone*. Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān read it that way: it stands as long as the disbelief does.
- **Reliance right where the break happens.** *Upon You we rely, to You we turn, to You is the return* is what Ibrahim and his companions said, in Ibn Kathir's words, "afterwards" — after parting with their people and disowning their way.
- **Concern for how the truth is read.** The reports of Mujāhid, Qatādah and Ibn ʿAbbās all locate the fear in the same place: that the believers' affliction would be taken as proof that the other side was right.
- **Seeking forgiveness alongside the stand.** *Waghfir lanā rabbanā* comes in the same breath as the plea for protection.
- **One firm boundary in the law:** forgiveness is not sought for those who died upon shirk — and Ibrahim's prayer for his father, which some of the believers themselves had cited as a precedent, is expressly ruled out as a proof for it.

And the last word of the passage keeps the whole thing in proportion. He is al-Ghanī and al-Ḥamīd — perfectly rich, and praiseworthy in all His statements and actions.

passages.title: Enmity that may soften, and the limits of loyalty
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the surah's great softening. After the command to be enemies with the disbelievers, Allah opens two doors at once: a door of hope, that today's enemy may become tomorrow's friend (ayah 7), and a door of conscience, that the ban on friendly intimacy was never a ban on kindness or fairness toward peaceable people (ayat 8-9). The line between the two is drawn by what people have actually done — whether they fought the believers over religion, drove them from their homes, or backed that expulsion — and, as the commentators insist, justice is owed either way.

## The wound these ayat came to heal

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The preceding verses had vehemently prohibited the Muslims from maintaining any friendly intimacy with non-believers, even where there were very near blood relationships. The noble Companions carried out the commands of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ in letter and spirit; in this matter they did not care about their personal desires or about their near and dear ones. The result was that in some homes the father was a Muslim and the son an unbeliever, or the reverse. Friendly relations were severed.

Maʿārif is honest about the cost: "Obviously, this situation was not easy for their human nature." That is the ache ayah 7 speaks into. Allah does not scold them for feeling it; He gives them the assurance that soon the hardship will be over. Maʿārif adds that according to some ahadith, when a servant of Allah gives up his favourite thing for the sake of Allah, Allah delivers it to him in a lawful manner, and at times he is granted something better than it.

## Ayah 7 — "Perhaps Allah will make friendship..."

Ibn Kathir notes exactly where this verse falls: "Allah said to His faithful servants, **after ordering them to be enemies with the disbelievers**..." The severed relationships, in other words, are not the end of the story.

**مَوَدَّة (mawaddah) — the friendship promised.** Ibn Kathir unpacks it in three strokes: "affection after animosity, tenderness after coldness and coming together after parting from each other." Set that beside Maʿārif's picture of households divided and relations cut off, and each phrase names a loss together with its reversal.

## "And Allah has power over all things"

**وَاللَّهُ قَدِيرٌ.** Ibn Kathir explains: "Allah is able to gather opposites and bring together hearts, after feeling hostility and hardness. In this case, the hearts will come together in agreement." This is the hinge of the promise. Reconciliation is not offered as a likely political outcome; it rests on Allah's power over the one thing no human power reaches — the inside of another person's chest.

Ibn Kathir proves it from history the audience had lived through. Of the Ansar, Allah said:

> "And remember Allah's favour on you, for you were enemies one to another but He joined your hearts together, so that, by His grace, you became brethren and were on the brink of a pit of Fire, and He saved you from it." (3:103)

And the Prophet ﷺ said to them: "Did I not find you misguided, and Allah guided you through me; and divided, and Allah united [your hearts] through me?"

Then the decisive verse:

> "He it is Who has supported you with His help and with the believers. And He has united their hearts. If you had spent all that is in the earth, you could not have united their hearts, but Allah has united them. Certainly He is Almighty, All-Wise." (8:62-63)

The point is stark: all the wealth on earth cannot buy the joining of two hearts. So a believer looking at an implacable enemy is not looking at a closed case. He is looking at something only Allah can change — and Allah is Qadīr, He has power over it.

## "And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful"

Why close a verse about enemies with forgiveness and mercy? Because that is the mechanism by which an enemy stops being one. Ibn Kathir: it means "Allah forgives the disbelief of the disbelievers if they repent from it, returned to their Lord and surrendered to Him in Islam. Surely, He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most-Merciful to those who repent to Him from their sins, no matter what type of the sin it is."

Read that last clause slowly. Even the disbelief itself is forgiven when they turn back — and no type of sin is placed outside the mercy of the One who is Ghafūr Raḥīm to whoever repents to Him.

## The promise came true

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads these verses as an indication of what was coming: those who were then the implacable enemies of the Muslims because of their disbelief would soon become their friends. In other words, Allah would grant the enemies the ability to embrace the Faith, and thus restore the mutual relationships. Citing Mazhari, Maʿārif states that this prophecy was fulfilled on the occasion of the Conquest of Makkah, when, besides the unbelievers who were killed, the rest of the people became Muslims. The Qur'an describes that moment: "and you see people entering Allah's religion in multitudes" (110:2).

## Hold your loves and hatreds lightly

Ibn Kathir cites here the Hadith: "Love your loved one moderately, because one day, he might become your enemy. Hate your hated one moderately, because one day, he might become your loved one." (The source introduces it simply as "the Hadith" without naming a collection.)

The hadith turns the verse's "perhaps" inward. Since where hearts end up is not ours to know or to govern, extremes of attachment and extremes of loathing both claim a certainty about tomorrow that no servant possesses. A believer keeps his hostility measured, and always open to being dissolved by Allah.

## Ayah 8 — Asmāʼ and her mother

Now the passage turns from hope to law, and it does so through a story about a daughter and her mother.

Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad reported from Asmāʼ bint Abī Bakr: "My mother, who was an idolatress at the time, came to me during the Treaty of Peace, the Prophet ﷺ conducted with the Quraysh. I came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, 'O Allah's Messenger! My mother came visiting, desiring something from me, should I treat her with good relations?' The Prophet ﷺ said: **'Yes. Keep good relation with your mother.'**" Ibn Kathir adds that the Two Sahihs recorded this Hadith. Maʿārif reports the incident from the Sahih of Bukhari — the mother arrived in Madinah from Makkah in the state of disbelief — and notes that according to a narration in the Musnad of Ahmad, this occurred when the peace treaty of Hudaybiyyah with the Makkan Quraysh had been concluded and was in force. Maʿārif records that the Prophet ﷺ advised Asmāʼ to treat her mother kindly, politely and courteously, and that this verse was revealed on that occasion.

Ibn Kathir also records from Imam Ahmad, on the authority of ʿAbdullah bin Zubayr, the fuller picture: the mother, Qutaylah, came visiting with gifts — Dibāb, cheese and clarified butter — while still an idolatress. Asmāʼ refused to accept her mother's gifts and did not let her enter her house. ʿĀʼishah asked the Prophet ﷺ about his verdict, Allah sent down this ayah, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered Asmāʼ to accept her mother's gifts and to let her enter her house.

Maʿārif adds a family detail, from Ibn Kathir and Mazhari: some reports indicate that Qutaylah had been divorced by Abū Bakr in the Days of Ignorance, and that ʿĀʼishah was born of Abū Bakr's other wife, Umm Raman, who had embraced Islam.

Feel the shape of this. A question was raised, and revelation itself drew the boundary of the earlier command: the door of the house opens, the gifts are accepted, the tie with the mother is kept.

## What ayah 8 permits, in its own words

"Allah does not forbid you with those who fought not against you on account of religion nor drove you out of your homes..." Ibn Kathir glosses the second clause as meaning "those who did not have a role in your expulsion," and concludes: "Therefore, Allah does not forbid you from being kind to the disbelievers who do not fight you because of the religion, such as women and weak disbelievers."

Two things are then named, and they are not the same thing:

- **أَن تَبَرُّوهُمْ**, rendered "to deal kindly." Ibn Kathir: "to be gentle with them."
- **وَتُقْسِطُوا إِلَيْهِمْ**, rendered "and justly." Ibn Kathir: "to be fair with them."

The ayah permits both the warm thing and the exact thing — and then crowns the second: **"Verily, Allah loves those who deal with equity."** Justice toward such people is not a grudging concession; it is something Allah *loves*. Ibn Kathir recalls here what he calls the authentic Hadith: "The just, who are fair in their decisions, families and those under their authority, will be on podiums made of light, to the right of the Throne." (The source cites it as authentic without naming a collection.) Note its sweep — one's rulings, one's own family, and anyone placed under one's authority.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses further.** The verse directs that justice and good behaviour be maintained with those unbelievers who did not fight the Muslims. As for justice, Maʿārif says it is obligatory to maintain with *every* non-Muslim: whether a citizen of an Islamic State, or one with whom the Muslims have a peace agreement, or a citizen of an un-Islamic State, even though he is at war with the Muslims. Rather, Islam enjoins upon Muslims to do justice even to animals: we are not allowed to lay a burden on them more than they can bear, and we need to take care of their fodder and comfort. Given that baseline, Maʿārif concludes that the focus of the verse falls on the *additional* direction — that such people should be treated not only with justice, but also in a good and courteous manner.

**A ruling drawn from ayah 8** (Maʿārif): this verse proves that optional charities may be spent on non-Muslim citizens of an Islamic State and on non-Muslims with whom the Muslims have a peace pact. It is, however, forbidden to spend on non-believers who are at war with the Muslims.

## Ayah 9 — the limit, stated precisely

The verse is worded as a restriction — "**It is only** as regards those who..." — fencing the prohibition around one clearly described group. Maʿārif reads the verse the same way: it "merely forbids friendly intimacy and relations." Three descriptions are stacked:

1. those who **fought you on account of religion**,
2. those who **drove you out of your homes**,
3. those who **helped to drive you out**.

Maʿārif renders that third clause as those who "supported their expulsion" — so backing the aggression is named alongside waging it.

**أَن تَوَلَّوْهُمْ — "that you befriend them."** Ibn Kathir: "Allah forbids you from being kind and befriending with the disbelievers who are openly hostile to you, those who fought against you, expelled you and helped to expel you. Allah the Exalted forbids you from being their friends and orders you to be their enemy."

Then the warning: **"And whosoever will befriend them, then such are the wrongdoers."** Ibn Kathir sets this beside 5:51 — "O you who believe! Take not the Jews and the Christians as protecting friends, they are but protecting friends of each other. And if any among you takes them as protecting friends, then surely, he is one of them. Verily, Allah guides not those people who are the wrongdoers." The word the ayah uses is *ẓālimūn*, wrongdoers — the same word Allah uses in 5:51 of those He does not guide.

## How the scholars draw the line

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here, and its care is worth spelling out, because the two halves of the ruling are easily confused.

- **What is forbidden:** friendly or cordial intimacy — Maʿārif calls it "intimate and heart-felt friendship." And it states that this prohibition is *not* restricted only to those enemies who actively wage war against Muslims; it extends to *ahl al-dhimmah* (non-Muslim citizens of an Islamic State) and *ahl al-ṣulḥ* (non-Muslims with whom there is a peace pact). Such friendship is not allowed with them either.
- **What is not forbidden:** justice and good treatment. On the basis of this juristic principle, Maʿārif reports, Mazhari ruled that justice, equity and fairness are necessary *even with the hostile disbelievers who are at war with the Muslims*. The prohibition applies only in the case of cordial and friendly intimacy, not in the case of a courteous attitude and kindness — which shows, Maʿārif says, that it is permissible to be polite and courteous even to those hostile enemies who are at war with the Muslims.
- **The one caveat:** treating them with tenderness and courtesy should not cause danger, threat, or loss to the Muslims. Wherever courtesy or tenderness might pose such a danger, it is not permitted. "Of course, justice and equity in all cases and under all circumstances are necessary and imperative."

So the two things a modern reader tends to fuse — *intimate alliance* and *decency* — are separated in the commentary itself. Ayah 9 forbids the first. Ayah 8 commands the second. Neither cancels the other.

## Living it

- **Judge by conduct, not by label.** The criterion the ayat name is behaviour: did they fight you over your religion, drive you from your homes, or help drive you out? Ibn Kathir's own examples of those covered by ayah 8 are "the disbelievers who do not fight you because of the religion, such as women and weak disbelievers."
- **Give kindness and fairness their full weight.** Being gentle and being fair are not loopholes reluctantly permitted; Allah says He *loves* those who deal with equity — and Maʿārif holds justice obligatory with every non-Muslim without exception.
- **Keep relatives' rights intact.** The Prophet's ﷺ instruction to Asmāʼ — "Keep good relation with your mother" — settles the case of the non-Muslim parent: the gift is accepted, the door is opened, the tie is kept.
- **Guard the heart's loyalty.** What ayah 9 withholds is intimate, heart-felt friendship with those who fought your faith and expelled you, or backed that expulsion.
- **Never write anyone off.** Maʿārif reads ayah 7 as spoken about people who were then implacable enemies of the Muslims, and says the promise was fulfilled at the Conquest of Makkah. Allah is Qadīr — able to join hearts that all the wealth of the earth could not join — and Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful to whoever repents to Him, no matter what type of sin it is. So hold your estrangements loosely; Allah may yet make between you the affection this ayah promises.

passages.title: Emigrant women, severed marriages, and the return of dowries
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat settle a painful, concrete problem thrown up by the treaty of Hudaybiyyah: what to do when a woman fled Makkah for her faith, and the treaty seemed to say she must be handed back. Allah's answer runs through both ayat as one ruling — test her sincerity, never return her, recognise that her marriage to an idolater is already dissolved, then settle the money honestly on both sides; ayah 11 handles the case where the other party refuses to settle at all.

## The treaty that made this necessary

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. After long negotiation, a ten-year peace was concluded between the Quraysh of Makkah and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Some terms were accepted only under pressure; the Muslims felt subdued, and the Companions expressed extreme grief and indignation. But the Prophet ﷺ was acting under divine direction, knowing this apparent defeat was the prelude to "a clear victory" — and eventually the Companions accepted it too.

One clause was the sting. Ibn Kathir preserves its wording, reported by ʿUrwah, Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd, Az-Zuhrī, Muqātil bin Ḥayyān and As-Suddī: "Every man (in another narration, every person) who reverts from our side to your side, should be returned to us, even if he is a follower of your religion." Traffic the other way was not returned. On its face the wording was general: any person, man or woman.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recounts that while the Prophet ﷺ was still at Hudaybiyyah, Sayyidnā Abū Jandal ؓ — held captive by the Quraysh in Makkah — escaped and appeared in the Muslim camp with his feet still in fetters. Handing an oppressed brother back to his oppressors felt intolerable; yet the treaty had been concluded, and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the firmness of the principles of the Sharīʿah could not be sacrificed for one individual. The Prophet ﷺ, who surely felt natural grief at this, explained the situation to him and sent him back — foreseeing what lay ahead for the oppressed believers.

The men were being returned. Then the women began to arrive.

## The women who came

The sources preserve more than one such arrival, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes there is no contradiction between them — possibly all of them happened.

**Sayyidah Sāʿidah bint al-Ḥārith al-Aslamiyyah ؓ** was a Muslim woman married to a non-believer (Ṣayfī Ibn Anṣab, or in some reports Musāfir al-Makhzūmī); until then marriage between Muslims and non-Muslims was not forbidden. She escaped Makkah and came to the Prophet ﷺ. Her husband followed and demanded her return, pointing out that the seal on the treaty was still fresh. On that occasion these ayat were revealed — so Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Qurṭubī, on the authority of Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās ؓ.

**Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqbah bin Abī Muʿayṭ ؓ** emigrated and her two brothers, ʿUmārah and Al-Walīd, came after her. Ibn Kathir cites ʿAbdullāh bin Abī Aḥmad — from his biography in Al-Musnad Al-Kabīr — that they came to Allah's Messenger ﷺ asking for her return, and Allah abolished the part of the treaty concerning women specifically, forbidding that Muslim women be sent back and revealing the ayah about testing them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that in some reports her husband ʿAmr Ibn al-ʿĀṣ (not yet a Muslim) came to Madinah to take her back; the two brothers were returned under the treaty, but she was not — the Prophet ﷺ saying the clause applied to men and not to women, after which the ayat came down confirming his reading.

Ibn Kathir also records from **the Sahih**, on the report of Al-Miswar and Marwān bin Al-Ḥakam, that after the treaty with the Quraysh some Muslim women emigrated to the Prophet ﷺ, and Allah sent down this ayah about them, up to "do not keep disbelieving women."

## Was this a breach of the treaty?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this head-on. On Qurṭubī's narration, the clause — though generally worded — never covered women in the Prophet's ﷺ understanding; he clarified that at Hudaybiyyah, and the ayat came to confirm it. On other reports he had gone along with the general wording, these ayat restricted it, and he then made the exemption clear to the Quraysh there and then.

Either way, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, this was neither a breach nor a termination of the treaty but a clarification of the clause's true import — and the proof is what followed: both parties continued to treat the treaty as valid and acted on it for a time. Roads became safe, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrote to the kings and emperors of the world, and Abū Sufyān's caravan travelled freely into Syrian territory, where Heraclius summoned him to enquire about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Ibn Kathir frames the same point in terms of how the ayah relates to the Sunnah: on the reports above, the ayah **specifies and explains** the Sunnah — narrowing a general ruling rather than cancelling it — "and this is the best case of understanding." Yet, he notes, another view among some of the Salaf is that it **abrogates** it. Both views are recorded; the sources do not force a choice.

## "Test them" — ayah 10

**فَٱمْتَحِنُوهُنَّ — "examine them."** The exemption rests on faith, so faith had to be verified. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the risk plainly: a woman might have fled Makkah not for her religion but out of anger with her husband, or love of someone in Madinah, or some other worldly motive. Such a woman is not exempt and must be returned.

What did the test consist of?

- **Ibn ʿAbbās ؓ**, in Al-ʿAwfī's report cited by Ibn Kathir, said their examination was to ask them to testify that there is no deity but Allah and that Muhammad is Allah's servant and His Messenger.
- **Mujāhid** said: ask them why they migrated; if they came because they were angry with their husbands, or for some other reason, and you realised they had not embraced the faith, send them back to their husbands.
- **Ibn ʿAbbās ؓ**, in the report Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes from Qurṭubī, describes an oath: the woman would swear she had not come out of hatred for her husband, nor love of any man in Madinah, nor for any worldly reason, but purely for the sake of Allah and for love of His Messenger ﷺ. Once she swore, the Prophet ﷺ would let her stay and would return to her disbelieving husband the dower he had spent on her.
- **Sayyidah Ṣiddīqah ؓ** reported — as recorded in **Tirmidhī**, who grades it *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ* — that the method of testing was the pledge of allegiance (*bayʿah*) described a little later in ayah 12: "when the believing women come to you, seeking bayʿah with you."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān harmonises these: possibly she first swore the oath, then completed the matter with the pledge on the blessed hands of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — "and Allah knows best."

**"Allah knows best about their faith."** Real faith lives in the heart, which none but Allah knows; what people can do is estimate it from verbal confession and circumstantial evidence, and Muslims are legally obliged to do just that much. At the same time, Ibn Kathir observes on "**if you ascertain that they are true believers**" that the ayah shows faith *can* be recognised and affirmed.

## The marriage bond itself is severed

**"They are not lawful for the disbelievers nor are the disbelievers lawful for them."** This explains *why* the woman is not returned: there is nothing to return her to. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the ruling directly — a woman married to an unbeliever who then embraces Islam while he does not has her marriage tie dissolved *ipso facto*, by the fact itself.

Ibn Kathir stresses how new this was: the ayah forbids Muslim women to idolaters, "which was a lawful marriage in the beginning of Islam." He illustrates the earlier state of affairs from the Prophet's ﷺ own family. His daughter **Zaynab ؓ** was married to **Abū al-ʿĀṣ bin Ar-Rabīʿ**, she a Muslim and he an idolater with his people. Captured at Badr, his ransom was sent by Zaynab — a necklace that had belonged to Khadījah ؓ. The Prophet ﷺ became very emotional at the sight of it and told the Companions that if they saw fit to release her prisoner, they should do so. They did, and he was freed on condition that he send Zaynab to Allah's Messenger ﷺ. Abū al-ʿĀṣ kept his word and sent her with Zayd bin Ḥārithah. She remained in Madinah from Badr in year two of the Hijrah until he embraced Islam in year eight — and then, Ibn Kathir notes, she returned to their marriage without a new dower.

**"And do not hold on to the ties of marriage with the disbelieving women."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the words: *ʿiṣam* is the plural of *ʿiṣmah*, whose root sense is protection or bond, here the protected bond of marriage; *kawāfir* is the plural of *kāfirah*, a pagan woman. It cannot mean a *kitābiyyah* — a woman of a previously revealed scripture, Jewish or Christian — since marrying her is permitted by explicit Qur'anic text. So marriages with pagan women, permitted until now, were forbidden going forward and existing ones cancelled.

Ibn Kathir records the response: when this was revealed, **ʿUmar bin Al-Khaṭṭāb ؓ** divorced two of his wives who were idolatresses; one later married Muʿāwiyah bin Abī Sufyān and the other Ṣafwān bin Umayyah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (from al-Baghawī, on Zuhrī, as quoted by Mazharī) adds that these two had stayed behind in Makkah at the migration, and notes a precision: "divorce" here means severing the relationship, since technical *ṭalāq* was not needed — the ayah itself had already broken the bond.

**When may she remarry?** Ibn Kathir notes the ordinary conditions still apply: her ʿiddah (waiting period) must be complete and she must have a legal guardian for the marriage. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives Imām Abū Ḥanīfah's رح framework: where the wife becomes Muslim and the husband remains an unbeliever, the Muslim ruler should call on him to accept Islam; if he does, the marriage continues; if he refuses, the ruler separates them and she may marry whom she wishes. But a ruler can only summon a man inside an Islamic land. Where the husband is in non-Muslim territory, separation is instead accomplished by her migrating to the Islamic State or joining the Muslim army base — the jurists' principle of *ikhtilāf ud-dārayn*, "the difference of the two abodes."

## Settling the money

**"But give them that which they have spent."** The disbelieving husband gets his dower back. Ibn Kathir attributes this reading to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, Az-Zuhrī and others. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a striking observation about *who* is addressed: not the emigrant woman — she may well have spent it and have nothing left — but the Muslim community as a whole, best paid from the public treasury (*bayt al-māl*), or else by the contributions of the Muslims (Qurṭubī). The obligation of honouring the treaty was carried collectively, not dumped on a refugee.

**"And there is no sin on you to marry them, when you give them their dowers."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the dower is mentioned as though it were a condition, when the jurists unanimously hold that a marriage's validity does not depend on paying the mahr (though paying it is obligatory at or after marriage). It forestalls a natural confusion: a mahr had just been paid out on this woman's account, so a man marrying her might imagine the matter settled. The ayah clarifies that the earlier mahr belonged to the earlier marriage; a new marriage requires a new one.

**"And ask for what you have spent, and let them ask for what they have spent."** Symmetry: Ibn Kathir glosses it as asking back what you paid to wives who went over to the idolaters, while they are entitled to recover the dowers they gave to the wives who emigrated to the Muslims. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the sums owed each way were to be settled by mutual reckoning of the accounts — and records how it went in practice: the Muslims acted on this willingly, because they held adherence to the Qur'an binding, and paid back the mahr to every unbelieving husband who had paid it; the pagans of Makkah did not believe in the Qur'an, so they did not act on it. That refusal, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, is the occasion on which the next ayah was revealed.

**"That is the judgement of Allah; He judges between you."** Ibn Kathir: this ruling about the treaty and the exclusion of women from its clauses is a decision Allah made for His creation. **"And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"** — He knows what benefits His servants and is Most Wise concerning it.

## Ayah 11: when the other side will not pay

Ayah 11 is Allah's provision for exactly that refusal: "And if any of your wives have gone from you to the disbelievers — then *ʿāqabtum* — then pay those whose wives have gone the equivalent of what they had spent."

The whole ayah turns on one verb, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out three readings:

1. **From *muʿāqabah*, "to retaliate"** — reported from Qatādah, Mujāhid and Qurṭubī. The pagans were bound to refund the Muslim husbands' dowers as the Muslims had refunded theirs; since they defaulted, the believers may withhold an equivalent amount from what they owed, and that withheld money goes to the husbands who lost wives.
2. **"To acquire spoils of war"** — the verb is read in variant recitations (*qirāʾāt*) as *ʿaqabtum*, *ʿaqqabtum* and *aʿqabtum*, and Qatādah and Mujāhid held all three forms carry this sense. Then the meaning is that the defrauded husbands are compensated out of war booty.
3. **From *ʿāqibah*, "turn"** — as in taking turns riding a mount; so "when your turn to pay comes round." Instead of paying the unbelievers, pay it to the Muslims whose wives left and whose dowers were never returned. Ālūsī in *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī* and Mawlānā Ashraf Thānawī رح adopt this, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own translation follows it.

Ibn Kathir preserves the early authorities' application of the ayah. Mujāhid and Qatādah applied it to disbelievers who had no peace treaty: if a woman flees to them and they withhold what her husband spent, then when a woman comes to the Muslims nothing is returned to her husband until they pay the Muslim his equivalent.

Az-Zuhrī's report in Ibn Jarīr records what actually happened and then gives the mechanism. What happened: the believers abided by Allah's decree and paid what they owed the idolaters to compensate for the dowers the idolaters had given the emigrant women, while the idolaters refused to accept Allah's judgement for what they owed the Muslims. The mechanism: so if a Muslim woman reverts to the idolaters, her Muslim husband is repaid out of whatever money remains with the believers from the dowers of the women who migrated to them — money that was owed to those women's idolater husbands; and if anything is still owed to the idolaters after that, it must be returned to them.

Notice the restraint: even in retaliation no one takes more than the equivalent, and any surplus still goes back to the enemy. Hence the closing words, **"And have taqwā of Allah, the One in Whom you are believers."** Money owed to a hostile party that is itself cheating is precisely where taqwā is tested — and the ayah appeals to the very thing that sets the believers apart from the Quraysh: you actually believe in Him.

## Did Muslim women really apostatise?

Since ayah 11 speaks of wives going over to the disbelievers, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks how often this occurred. Some authorities say it arose in a single case: Umm-ul-Ḥakam bint Abī Sufyān, wife of Sayyidnā ʿIyāḍ Ibn Ghanam Quraishī, left the faith and fled to Makkah — though she later returned to Islam.

Ibn ʿAbbās ؓ reports that about six women in all abandoned Islam and went over to the unbelievers. On the analysis Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives from Qurṭubī, only that one truly apostatised and fled; the other five had been unbelievers from the outset and remained in Makkah at the migration, and when this ayah dissolved their marriages they clung stubbornly to disbelief. They too were counted among those whose dowers the Makkans owed to Muslim husbands — and when the Makkans did not pay, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ compensated those husbands from the spoils of war. Baghawī, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās ؓ as quoted by Mazharī, reports that all five later came to Islam.

## What the passage asks of us

**Faith outranks blood, treaty and marriage — but not justice.** A woman who arrived with nothing but her belief was given sanctuary against the letter of a signed agreement. In the same breath, her former husband — an idolater and an enemy — was paid every coin he was owed, by a community that took the bill on itself.

**Judge by what is apparent, and leave hearts to Allah.** The test was real and had to be passed; but the ayah's own comment, "Allah knows best about their faith," fences off any pretence that we can see inside another person.

**Keep the accounts clean when the other side does not.** The believers paid; the Quraysh refused; and the redress Allah legislated was measured to the exact equivalent and sealed with a command to taqwā. Where a wrong is genuinely owed you, the limit of redress is what you actually lost — not what anger suggests.

passages.title: The women's pledge and the final warning
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat close Sūrat al-Mumtaḥanah. In ayah 12 Allah instructs His Prophet ﷺ on how to receive the believing women who come to give him their *bayʿah* — their pledge of allegiance — and lists six commitments they undertake. In ayah 13 the surah returns to where it began, warning the believers not to take as allies a people who have earned Allah's anger. What binds the two together is a single question of loyalty: ayah 12 shows loyalty being *given* — to Allah, to His Messenger ﷺ, to a way of life spelled out clause by clause; ayah 13 shows loyalty being *withheld* — from those who have no hope left in the Hereafter.

## From testing to pledging

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places ayah 12 directly against ayah 10. There, Allah had directed that when emigrant women arrive from Makkah, the believers should test and examine them. The pledge in ayah 12, Maʿārif says, is the complement to that test: first their faith is verified, then their commitment is formally taken. And this pledge is not only about belief in the abstract — it binds the Muslim woman to the practical precepts of Islam as well.

But the wording of the ayah is general. It does not say "the emigrant women"; it says "the believing women." So Maʿārif concludes that it covers all Muslim women, not just new arrivals — and this is exactly what happened in practice. When the pledge was actually taken, the women who had been Muslim all along joined in too, as recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ of Bukhārī on the authority of Umm ʿAṭiyyah, and by Baghawī from Umaymah bint Ruqayqah.

Maʿārif adds that this pledge of the women was not a one-off event after Ḥudaybiyah. It was taken several times afterwards, including on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. There the Prophet ﷺ first took the pledge of the men, then took it from the women at mount Ṣafā, with ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb relaying the words of the pledge on his behalf to the women gathered at the foot of the mountain. Among them was Hind, the wife of Abū Sufyān. She was at first embarrassed and wanted to keep herself hidden — but because the pledge contained real rulings of the Sharīʿah, she was drawn into speaking and asked several questions about them. (Mazharī, cited in Maʿārif, gives the incident in detail.)

## A pledge with no handshake

The most striking thing the sources preserve about this scene is what did *not* happen.

Al-Bukhārī recorded that ʿĀʾishah, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, said that Allah's Messenger ﷺ used to examine the women who migrated to him according to this very ayah, reciting from *"O Prophet! When believing women come to you pledging to you…"* through to *"Verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."* ʿUrwah reports her saying: when a believing woman agreed to these conditions, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would say to her, **قَدْ بَايَعْتُكِ** — *"I have accepted your pledge."* Then ʿĀʾishah adds: *by Allah, he never touched the hand of any woman at all while taking the pledge from them.* He took their pledge by speech alone.

A separate report, recorded by Imam Aḥmad from Umaymah bint Ruqayqah, preserves the moment the women themselves raised the question. She said: "I came to Allah's Messenger ﷺ with some women to give him our pledge, and he took from us the pledge mentioned in the Qurʼān…" In the course of that meeting they said, "O Messenger of Allah, should you not shake hands with us?" He ﷺ replied: **إِنِّي لَا أُصَافِحُ النِّسَاءَ، إِنَّمَا قَوْلِي لِامْرَأَةٍ وَاحِدَةٍ كَقَوْلِي لِمِائَةِ امْرَأَةٍ** — *"I do not shake hands with women; my statement to one woman is as my statement to a hundred women."* Ibn Kathīr notes this ḥadīth has an authentic chain and that at-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah collected it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the contrast: the men's pledge was sealed by the hand; the women's loyalty was a verbal pledge, without touching the blessed hand of the Messenger ﷺ. Citing Mazharī, Maʿārif states that his blessed hand never touched the hand of any non-*maḥram* woman (a woman he was not permanently forbidden to marry). A boundary was kept, and the covenant was still fully sealed — his word to one, as he told them, being as his word to a hundred.

## The six conditions

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts six commitments in ayah 12, and observes that they concern matters in which laxity commonly creeps in, which is why they were spelled out rather than left implied.

**1. That they associate nothing with Allah.** This is the foundation — affirmation of faith and the rejection of *shirk* — and Maʿārif notes it is a vow common to men and women alike. Everything after it is built on it.

**2. That they will not steal.** Ibn Kathīr explains this as the property of other people. He then adds an important qualification. If a husband is not fulfilling his duty of financial support, his wife may take a reasonable amount from his wealth for her own needs — whether he knows of it or not — because of the ḥadīth recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs in which Hind bint ʿUtbah said, "O Messenger of Allah, Abū Sufyān is a miser; he does not give me enough for our family's living expenses and my own. May I take from his money without his knowledge?" He ﷺ answered: **خُذِي مِنْ مَالِهِ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ، مَا يَكْفِيكِ وَيَكْفِي بَنِيكِ** — *"Take from it what is reasonable and appropriate for you and your children."* So "theft" here is taking what is not one's right; a wife's rightful maintenance is not that.

**3. That they will not commit zinā.** Ibn Kathīr connects this to *"And come not near to zinā; verily it is an immoral act and an evil way"* (17:32), and mentions a ḥadīth collected from Samurah that for adulterers and fornicators there is a painful torment in the Fire. Maʿārif adds a communal observation: when women are firm in this, men's salvation from the same sin becomes easier — chastity is a shared shelter, not one person's private burden.

There is a beautiful human moment here. Imam Aḥmad recorded from ʿĀʾishah that Fāṭimah bint ʿUtbah came to give her pledge, and when the Prophet ﷺ took from her the clauses about *shirk*, theft and zinā, she bashfully placed her hand on her head in shyness — and the Prophet ﷺ *liked* what she did. ʿĀʾishah said to her, "O woman! Accept the pledge — by Allah, we all gave the pledge to the same." She said, "Yes then," and gave her pledge to the same things mentioned in the ayah.

**4. That they will not kill their children.** Ibn Kathīr says this includes killing children after they are born — the people of Jāhiliyyah used to kill their children because they feared poverty — and he states that the ayah also includes killing the fetus, as some ignorant women do for various evil reasons. Maʿārif recalls the specific practice of the Days of Ignorance: burying infant girls alive. This clause of the pledge is a bar placed across that road.

**5. That they will not bring *buhtān*.** *Buhtān* is calumny — a fabricated accusation. Ibn ʿAbbās explained the ayah's clause as meaning that they not attribute to their husbands children other than their legitimate ones; Muqātil said the same. Maʿārif reports that the commentators describe this happening in three ways: a woman claims a child born to her from another man is her husband's; she takes custody of another child and claims it is her husband's; or — Allah forbid — she commits adultery, conceives, and then imputes the child to her husband. In short, Maʿārif says, false ascription of paternity is forbidden in any form whatsoever. And though the ayah names this case, Maʿārif stresses that the word *buhtān* is used in its general sense: calumny is totally forbidden, whether against the husband, any other person, or even a non-believer — though it is graver still when directed at the husband.

**6. That they will not disobey you in what is *maʿrūf*.** This last clause is a general rule that gathers up everything not named. It means, Ibn Kathīr says, that they will obey him ﷺ when he orders them to do good and forbids them from evil. Al-Bukhārī recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said of it, "This was one of the conditions which Allah imposed on the women."

## "Between their hands and their feet"

The wording of the fifth clause is unusual and deserves a pause: *"they will not utter slander, fabricating it between their hands and their feet."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this phrase was added to indicate that on the Day of Resurrection a person's own hands and feet will bear witness against his actions. The ayah thus warns, Maʿārif says, that the one who commits such sins is committing them *in the presence of four witnesses* who will one day testify against him.

## The limit on obedience

Maymūn ibn Mihrān said, "Allah did not order obedience to His Prophet for other than *maʿrūf* — and *maʿrūf* is itself obedience." Ibn Zayd said, "Allah commanded that His Messenger, the best of His creation, be obeyed in that which is *maʿrūf*."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses on why the qualifier is there at all, given that the Messenger ﷺ would only ever command people to do what is right and good. Its answer is that the phrase makes the Muslims in general understand clearly a permanent principle: **obedience to any created being in disobedience to Allah is absolutely forbidden** — so much so that even obedience to the Prophet ﷺ himself has been qualified by this condition. Maʿārif offers a second possible reason too: that the restriction blocks the way against Shayṭān whispering evil thoughts and creating deviant paths for a person to go astray.

Maʿārif also notes a difference in form: the men's pledge was generally taken in concise terms, about faith and Islam — because men's pledging of faith and obedience already secures an undertaking to practise the entire system of the Sharīʿah, so details were not needed. The women's pledge spelled the details out. But this was not a permanent divide: as time went on, the same detailed pledge came to be taken from men as well, as the Prophetic reports transmitted by ʿUbādah ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit confirm (Qurṭubī).

## What "maʿrūf" covered in practice

The reports show the pledge being applied at once to a specific custom of grief. Al-Bukhārī recorded that Umm ʿAṭiyyah said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took our pledge and recited to us the ayah *'that they will not associate anything with Allah'* — and forbade us to wail for the dead." Thereupon a lady withdrew her hand, saying, "But such-and-such a lady shared with me in lamenting over one of my relatives, so I must reward hers." The Prophet ﷺ did not object; she went there, returned, and he accepted her pledge. Muslim also collected this ḥadīth. Ibn Jarīr's version of the report from Umm ʿAṭiyyah al-Anṣāriyyah adds that only she and Umm Sulaym bint Milḥān, the mother of Anas ibn Mālik, did this — and al-Bukhārī collected the ḥadīth by way of Ḥafṣah bint Sīrīn from Umm ʿAṭiyyah Nusaybah al-Anṣāriyyah.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from Asīd ibn Abī Asīd al-Barrād that one of the women who gave the pledge said: among the conditions of the pledge the Messenger took from us was that we do not disobey any act of *maʿrūf* he ordains — that we neither scratch our faces, nor pull our hair in grief, nor tear our clothes, nor wail.

## "As much as you can bear"

Imam Aḥmad's report from Umaymah bint Ruqayqah preserves the Prophet's ﷺ own softening of the terms. After taking the pledge he ﷺ said: **فِيمَا اسْتَطَعْتُنَّ وَأَطَقْتُنَّ** — *"as much as you can bear to implement."* The women answered, "Surely Allah and His Messenger are more merciful with us than we are with ourselves."

Umaymah's own reflection, as Maʿārif relays it from Mazharī, is worth sitting with: this shows that the Prophet ﷺ had more mercy and compassion for them than they had for themselves — they had wanted to pledge without any restriction or condition at all, and by uttering this sentence he reduced the burden and tension of the terms of loyalty, so that they would not be held guilty for a violation under compelled circumstances. That mercy runs in the same direction as the ayah's closing words: *"and ask Allah to forgive them. Verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."* The pledge is taken, and in the same breath forgiveness is sought for the one taking it.

## What happens if the pledge is broken

Imam Aḥmad recorded from ʿUbādah ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit that while they were with the Prophet ﷺ he said, "Pledge to me that you will not associate any with Allah, nor steal, nor commit zinā, nor kill your children" — then he recited this ayah and took the pledge from the women. He ﷺ then added: *"Those among you who fulfil this pledge will receive their reward from Allah. Those who deviate from any of it and receive the legal punishment in this life — the punishment will be an expiation for that sin. And whoever deviates from any of it and Allah screens him, then it is up to Allah to punish or forgive if He wills."* Ibn Kathīr notes the Two Ṣaḥīḥs recorded this ḥadīth.

This is the pledge's balance sheet, and it is neither loose nor crushing. Fulfilment is rewarded by Allah Himself. A worldly punishment already borne is an expiation. A concealed sin is left to Allah — which is precisely why the ayah ends by telling the Prophet ﷺ to seek forgiveness for those who pledge.

## Ayah 13: the surah closes where it opened

Ibn Kathīr's opening remark on ayah 13 is the key to reading it: **just as at the beginning of the surah, Allah forbids at the end of it taking the disbelievers as protecting friends.** The surah is framed by the same command; everything in between — the testing of the emigrant women, the rulings that follow, the pledge — sits inside that frame.

*"O you who believe! Take not as friends the people who incurred the wrath of Allah."* Ibn Kathīr says this refers to the Jews, Christians and the rest of the disbelievers whom Allah became angry with and cursed — those who deserved being rejected and banished by Him. The argument he draws out of the ayah is essentially a question put to the believer: how can you become their allies, friends and companions, after Allah has decided that they earn the despair of receiving any good or delights in the Hereafter?

The comparison at the end — *"just as the disbelievers have despaired of those buried in graves"* — carries two possible meanings, and Ibn Kathīr gives both:

- **First:** the disbelievers despair of ever again meeting their relatives buried in graves, because they do not believe in Resurrection or in being brought back to life. According to their own creed, there is no reunion left to hope for.
- **Second:** the disbelievers who are *already buried in the graves* have lost hope of receiving any kind of goodness — after seeing the punishment and knowing that the Resurrection was true.

On the second reading, Ibn Kathīr reports through al-Aʿmash, from Abū aḍ-Ḍuḥā, from Masrūq, that Ibn Masʿūd explained it as: *just as the disbeliever despairs when he dies and realises and knows his recompense.* Ibn Kathīr lists Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Muqātil, Ibn Zayd, al-Kalbī and Manṣūr as saying the same, and notes that Ibn Jarīr preferred this explanation.

Either way the image is of hope that has run out completely — the flat, final despair of someone standing at a grave with no belief in resurrection, or of someone in the grave who now sees what is coming.

## Living it

The passage ends the surah by putting two things side by side that the believer must hold together.

**Loyalty is specific, not sentimental.** Ayah 12 does not accept a vague declaration of goodwill. It names six things: worship Allah alone, do not take what is not yours, guard your chastity, do not kill your children, do not fabricate slander — least of all a false ascription of a child's parentage — and do not disobey in what is right. A commitment that cannot be itemised has not really been made.

**Obedience always has a ceiling, and the ceiling is Allah.** The clause *"in what is maʿrūf"* is the passage's safeguard. As Maʿārif puts it, obedience to any creation in disobedience to Allah is absolutely forbidden.

**Mercy is written into the terms.** *"As much as you can bear."* *"Ask Allah to forgive them."* *"Verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."* The One who set these conditions knows the weakness of the one keeping them, and has already provided for the failures.

**And the shape of your loyalties is not a private matter.** Ayah 13 closes the surah where it began: do not give your inmost allegiance to a people upon whom Allah's wrath has fallen, who have despaired of the Hereafter entirely. Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best.
